title: De motu vibratorio laminarum elasticarum, ubi plures novae vibrationum species hactenus non pertractatae evolvuntur

deep.reconstruction:
Problem: transverse vibration of a free–free elastic lamina EF held by a pin (stylus) at an interior point C, with EC = α and FC = β. Each portion obeys the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation. Euler separates variables with time factor cos(θθt). With Φ = θx/b he writes y = cos θθt (A cos Φ + B sin Φ + C e^Φ + D e^{-Φ}), and does the same for the other portion with primed letters. x is measured from E toward C and x' from F toward C.

Conditions gathered on the previous page:
- Free ends: y'' = y''' = 0 at x = 0, giving −A + C + D = 0 and −B + C − D = 0. The same holds for the primed set.
- Pin: y = 0 at C, i.e. at ζ = θα/b and ζ' = θβ/b.
These are six homogeneous equations in eight unknowns.

This page adds two matching conditions at C:
- Equation 7 (slope continuity): dy/dx = dy'/dx'.
- Equation 8 (common curvature, i.e. continuity of bending moment): y'' + y''' = 0 in Euler's sense, meaning the sum of the two second derivatives vanishes. Euler argues that a positive second derivative on one side means the curvature points up, while on the other side it means the curvature points down.
Both signs are consistent only if the ordinate y' of the second portion is reckoned with the opposite orientation to y (both abscissas run toward C, plus a reflected ordinate). Under that convention, slope continuity reads dy/dx = dy'/dx' and moment continuity reads y_xx + y'_x'x' = 0.

The third derivatives, whose jump at C gives the pin reaction (shear jump), are explicitly set aside as 'of small moment'.

The 8×8 homogeneous system has a nontrivial solution only if its determinant vanishes. That determinant is a single transcendental equation in ζ, ζ' with ζ:ζ' = α:β, so it fixes the frequencies.

Eliminating A, B, A', B' from the first six equations gives C/D = (−cos ζ + sin ζ − e^{−ζ})/(cos ζ + sin ζ + e^{ζ}), and likewise for the primed letters (next page). I verified this from A = C + D, B = C − D and y(α) = 0.

On the next page Euler declares the general case α ≠ β 'most difficult' and treats only the midpoint case. There the system splits as D' = ±D into two mode families. With each half being a free–pinned segment matched at C, these correspond in modern terms to:
- antisymmetric modes: each half acts as pinned–free, with frequency equation tan ζ = tanh ζ;
- symmetric modes: each half acts as clamped–free, with cos ζ cosh ζ = −1.
errors: Typographic slip in the eighth equation as printed: '−A' cos ζ' should be '−A' cos ζ'' (prime missing).
In the list of unknowns 'A', B', C', D' the last D lacks its prime.

The sign conventions (slopes equal, but second derivatives summing to zero) are only consistent if y' is measured with reversed orientation relative to y. With both abscissas running toward C and ordinates in the same sense, the slopes should be opposite and the curvatures equal. Euler's verbal justification for equation 8 is somewhat loose, but the resulting system is equivalent up to the sign of the primed coefficients, so the frequency equations are unaffected.
The previous page has 'B cos ζ'' for 'B' cos ζ'' in the formula for dy'/dx' (printing slip).

ideas.what: Interface (matching) conditions at an intermediate pin support of a vibrating beam: zero deflection on both sides, continuity of slope and of bending moment, shear jump = support reaction
ideas.modern_name: Transmission/interface conditions for the Euler–Bernoulli beam at an intermediate simple support (multi-span beam)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E443, 1773), within the Euler–D. Bernoulli tradition of beam vibration; later systematised in 19th-century multi-span beam theory (e.g. Clapeyron for statics)
ideas.where_published: E443 itself (Novi Comm. Petrop. 17, 1772/73); discussed by Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (Opera omnia II 11/2)

ideas.what: Frequency determination as vanishing of the determinant of an 8×8 homogeneous linear system, reduced to one transcendental equation because ζ:ζ' = α:β is given
ideas.modern_name: Characteristic (frequency) equation of a two-span free–free beam on a pin; transfer/determinant method
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler / D. Bernoulli for single spans; the general multi-span method is 19th–20th c. standard engineering

ideas.what: Remark that the third derivatives determine the force the stylus sustains, not pursued
ideas.modern_name: Support reaction from the shear-force jump

missed.claim: Euler sets up the full eigenvalue problem for a free–free beam pinned at an arbitrary point (α ≠ β) but abandons the general case as too difficult, solving only α = β. The general off-centre case (frequencies as functions of α/β, e.g. how the D'=±D families deform) is a routine 8×8 determinant today and is well covered in engineering vibration tables, so nothing substantive is missing from the literature.
missed.quote: quum ratio istorum angulorum ζ et ζ' detur, quippe quae est vt α ad β
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only historical interest: it marks where Euler stopped. The problem is fully solved in modern structural dynamics.

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains standard interface conditions for a pinned beam and a setup of the determinant. The content is known, attributed to E443 itself, and discussed by Truesdell; there is no hidden result.
transcription_corrections: Eighth equation: the original prints '−A'cof ζ' without prime on ζ (printer's slip); the transcription reproduces it as 'A'\cos\zeta', which is faithful.
Final list 'A', B', C', D' – the original also lacks the prime on D, so the transcription is faithful.
The catchword at page bottom is 'C/D =' as transcribed.
